words.childMeaning: Using few words to say something clearly.
practiceSentences: A concise covering letter is read; a long one is skimmed.
Can you make this concise without losing the argument?
Concise writing takes longer to produce than loose writing.
She rewrote the summary three times to make it concise.
Concise says it in few words; brief only means short.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Allowed by rules or law, or reasonable and justified.
practiceSentences: The company holds a legitimate licence for the work.
Is that a legitimate reason for refusing the request?
A legitimate complaint deserves an answer even when it is inconvenient.
Her legitimate expectation was set out in the contract.
Legitimate can mean lawful, or simply fair enough.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To protect something or someone from criticism, attack or harm.
practiceSentences: Be ready to defend every figure in the proposal.
How would you defend this decision to somebody who disagrees?
To defend a claim is to give the reasons, not to repeat it louder.
Imani defended her conclusion without once raising her voice.
A claim you cannot defend is a claim you should not have made.

words.group: Grammar: sentences that exclaim, and words that join equals
words.childMeaning: Describing a sentence that expresses strong feeling.
practiceSentences: What a difference a year makes is an exclamatory sentence.
Which exclamatory sentence would suit this ending?
An exclamatory sentence ends with an exclamation mark.
She cut every exclamatory sentence from the formal letter.
An exclamatory sentence exclaims; a declarative one states.

words.group: Grammar: sentences that exclaim, and words that join equals
words.childMeaning: Describing a word that joins two parts of equal weight.
practiceSentences: And, but and or are coordinating conjunctions.
Which coordinating conjunction fits this sentence?
A coordinating conjunction joins equals; neither clause depends on the other.
She used a coordinating conjunction where a full stop would have been stronger.
Coordinating joins equals; subordinating makes one depend on the other.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ition
words.childMeaning: A skill, quality, or certificate that makes someone suitable for a job.
practiceSentences: A recognised qualification in accounting opened doors that years of unrecorded experience could not.
Which qualification would help most if you wanted to work as a wildlife photographer?
"Experience matters," said the recruiter, "but without the right qualification your application stops at the first desk."
I plan to earn a lifeguarding qualification next summer so I can work at the community pool.
A qualification is also a limit added to a claim, as in a qualified apology.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ition
words.childMeaning: The act of knowing something again, or of publicly acknowledging it.
practiceSentences: Face recognition unlocks the phone in less than a second.
What recognition did the reporters receive for the investigation?
Recognition of a pattern is faster than reasoning about it.
The paper won recognition it had not sought.
Recognition can mean identifying something, or honouring somebody.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ition
words.childMeaning: The way something or someone is shown or described.
practiceSentences: The film's representation of the town annoyed everyone who lives there.
What representation of young people does this article offer?
A representation is always a choice about what to leave out.
The mural was a colourful representation of the many cultures within our school.
Representation also means speaking or acting on behalf of others.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: The art of using language to persuade.
practiceSentences: The speech was fine rhetoric and thin on evidence.
What rhetoric does this headline use?
Rhetoric is a skill, and a skill can be used either way.
She studied rhetoric to become harder to persuade.
Rhetoric is the craft of persuasion; propaganda is persuasion with the other side removed.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A mild word used in place of a blunt or unpleasant one.
practiceSentences: Letting staff go is a euphemism for dismissing them.
Which euphemism is this report hiding behind?
A euphemism softens the sentence and hides the fact.
She replaced every euphemism with the plain word and the piece changed entirely.
A euphemism is polite; a lie is not, but the distance can be short.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Using humour to expose and criticise something.
practiceSentences: The satirical column is the most read page in the paper.
Is this piece satirical or simply rude?
A satirical article attacks a target, not merely a mood.
Satirical writing needs its readers to know what is being mocked.
Satirical mocks in order to criticise; comic only wants a laugh.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: An imitation of a style, made to be funny.
practiceSentences: The sketch was a parody of the evening news.
What is this parody actually imitating?
A parody has to copy well before it can mock.
Their parody of the advert was shared more widely than the advert.
A parody imitates a style; a caricature exaggerates a person.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A picture or description that exaggerates features for effect.
practiceSentences: The caricature gave the minister an enormous chin.
Which feature does this caricature exaggerate?
A caricature works because it is recognisable and unfair.
The article was a caricature of a complicated argument.
A caricature exaggerates what is there; a fabrication invents it.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: The meaning underneath what is actually said.
practiceSentences: The subtext of the statement was that nobody would be blamed.
What is the subtext of this apology?
Subtext is what a careful reader hears and a quick one misses.
She read the subtext before she finished the first paragraph.
The text is what is written; the subtext is what is meant.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: False information spread without the spreader knowing it is wrong.
practiceSentences: Misinformation spreads faster than the correction that follows it.
How would you check a story before passing the misinformation on?
Misinformation is not a lie: the person sharing it believes it.
One screenshot without a date started weeks of misinformation.
Misinformation is spread in error; disinformation is spread on purpose.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Information describing other information, such as when a file was made.
practiceSentences: The photograph's metadata gave the date and the place.
What metadata does this document carry?
Metadata often reveals more than the file it describes.
Journalists checked the metadata before believing the image.
Metadata is data about data, which is why it is easy to forget.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: An image or figure standing for a person online.
practiceSentences: Her avatar is a drawing of a heron.
What does your choice of avatar tell a stranger?
An avatar hides a face and reveals a preference.
The forum required an avatar and a name that was not your own.
An avatar represents you; it is not a portrait of you.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A machine's ability to perform tasks that would need human thought.
practiceSentences: Artificial intelligence now writes the first draft of some news reports.
What tasks does this intelligence actually perform?
An intelligence that sounds confident is not thereby correct.
Intelligence also means information gathered about an opponent.
Human intelligence and machine intelligence are not the same thing.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A method by which a computer improves from data rather than from instructions.
practiceSentences: Machine learning finds patterns nobody wrote down.
What data was this learning system trained on?
A learning system repeats whatever bias its data contained.
The recommendations improved as the learning continued.
Learning also means what you do when you find out something new.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Describing software whose code anyone may read and change.
practiceSentences: The tool is open-source, so anyone can inspect what it does.
Why does open-source matter for trusting a program?
Open-source is not the same as free of charge.
They chose an open-source encyclopedia over a closed one.
Open-source publishes the code; proprietary keeps it hidden.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Information spread to push one point of view, often by hiding the other side.
practiceSentences: The advertisement was really propaganda, sharing only the facts that suited the company.
A few leaders claimed the scientists were spreading propaganda to seize the forest.
How can a careful reader tell honest reporting apart from clever propaganda?
"Propaganda hides one side of the story," the teacher explained to the class.
I now check several sources so that propaganda cannot fool me into a bad choice.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: The act of working to make a change in society or to help a cause.
practiceSentences: Her activism began with a letter to the local paper.
What activism has changed a law you benefit from?
Activism is patient work that occasionally looks sudden.
Online activism reaches further and commits less.
Activism seeks change; reporting seeks to describe it.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: All the people entitled to vote in an election.
practiceSentences: The electorate grew by forty thousand this year.
What does the electorate actually want here?
An electorate is a group defined by a right, not by an opinion.
Newspapers claim to speak for an electorate that never asked them to.
The electorate votes; the government governs.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A penalty imposed to make a country or person obey.
practiceSentences: The sanctions were lifted after the agreement was signed.
What sanction would actually change this behaviour?
A sanction is meant to cost more than the behaviour is worth.
Trade sanctions hurt the people before they reach the government.
Sanction is its own opposite: it also means to give official approval.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Unfairly favouring one side over another.
practiceSentences: The report was biased in what it left out, not in what it said.
Is this source biased, and does it declare it?
A biased account can contain nothing but true statements.
She read two biased papers to find the shape of the argument.
Biased leans one way; balanced gives each side its best case.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Based on personal feelings rather than on facts.
practiceSentences: A review is subjective and should say so.
Is that judgement subjective or can it be tested?
A subjective opinion is not thereby worthless.
She separated the subjective paragraphs from the reported ones.
Subjective comes from the person; objective from the thing.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Having a mistake or weakness that makes something less than perfect.
practiceSentences: The survey was flawed because only readers replied.
What makes this method flawed rather than merely limited?
A flawed study can still point in the right direction.
The argument is flawed at its second step.
Flawed means it has a fault; false means it is wrong.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Open to more than one meaning.
practiceSentences: The headline was ambiguous, and probably on purpose.
Which word makes this sentence ambiguous?
An ambiguous statement lets a speaker deny either reading.
She rewrote the ambiguous clause into two plain ones.
Ambiguous offers two clear meanings; vague offers none.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: To question something closely and searchingly.
practiceSentences: Interrogate the source before you quote it.
How would you interrogate this claim?
To interrogate a statistic is to ask who counted, and how.
She interrogated the data and found the missing month.
To interrogate is to question hard; to interview is to let somebody speak.

words.group: Grammar: words that join unequals, and pairs that work together
words.childMeaning: Describing a word that makes one clause depend on another.
practiceSentences: Because, although and unless are subordinating conjunctions.
Which subordinating conjunction fits this sentence?
A subordinating conjunction turns a clause into a part of another.
Journalists use subordinating clauses to bury what they would rather not stress.
Subordinating makes one clause depend; coordinating joins equals.

words.group: Grammar: words that join unequals, and pairs that work together
words.childMeaning: Describing a pair of words that work together in a sentence.
practiceSentences: Either and or are correlative conjunctions.
Which correlative pair would suit this sentence?
A correlative pair must match: neither goes with nor.
She used the correlative pair not only and but also in one sentence.
Correlative conjunctions come in pairs; coordinating ones stand alone.

units.title: The Digital World and Future Innovation

words.group: Word building: -ance, -ation and -ility
words.childMeaning: The importance of something, or how much it matters.
practiceSentences: The significance of the result was clear only after the second trial.
What is the significance of this date in the file?
Significance is not the same as size: a tiny change can matter enormously.
She explained the significance of the missing metadata.
In statistics, significance means a result is unlikely to be chance.

words.group: Word building: -ance, -ation and -ility
words.childMeaning: Concentrating on one narrow area of work or study.
practiceSentences: Her specialisation is the security of medical devices.
What specialisation would you choose in computing?
Specialisation buys depth and costs breadth.
Early specialisation can close doors you have not seen yet.
Specialisation narrows on purpose; a general training does not.

words.group: Word building: -ance, -ation and -ility
words.childMeaning: The quality of staying steady and not changing unexpectedly.
practiceSentences: The system ran for a year without losing stability.
What threatens the stability of this network?
Stability is boring, which is how you know it is working.
They chose stability over the newest version.
Stability resists change; rigidity cannot accept it.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Changing how an organisation works by moving it onto digital systems.
practiceSentences: Digitalisation turned three filing rooms into one server.
What has digitalisation cost the people who ran those rooms?
Digitalisation changes the work, not only the storage.
The hospital's digitalisation took four years and two false starts.
Digitising converts a document; digitalisation changes the whole process.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Using a physical feature, such as a fingerprint, to identify someone.
practiceSentences: Biometric locks read a fingerprint instead of a key.
What happens if biometric data is stolen?
A biometric cannot be changed once it has leaked.
The border post introduced biometric checks last year.
A password can be replaced; a biometric cannot.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: A shared record of transactions that is very hard to alter.
practiceSentences: A blockchain stores each record in a chain that would have to be rewritten whole.
What problem is a blockchain actually solving here?
A blockchain removes the need to trust one central keeper.
The land registry trialled a blockchain and kept the paper copies.
A blockchain makes a record hard to change; it does not make it true.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Making a file smaller so it takes less space to store or send.
practiceSentences: Compression cut the video to a third of its size.
What does this compression throw away?
Lossless compression keeps everything; lossy compression does not.
Heavy compression turned the photograph into visible squares.
Compression saves space and sometimes spends quality.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Turning coded information back into a readable form.
practiceSentences: Decryption needs the key, not merely the method.
How long would decryption take without the key?
Decryption is encryption run backwards, and only with permission.
The archive released the decryption key after fifty years.
Encryption locks the message; decryption opens it.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Working out where a device or person is on the Earth.
practiceSentences: Geolocation put the photograph within ten metres of the harbour.
What geolocation data does this app send?
Geolocation is useful, and it is also a record of where you have been.
She turned geolocation off before posting the picture.
Geolocation finds a position; a map only shows one.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: The ability of different systems to work together.
practiceSentences: Interoperability lets two hospitals read the same record.
Why is interoperability so often promised and so rarely delivered?
Interoperability needs an agreed standard more than it needs good code.
The lack of interoperability cost the project a year.
Interoperability is systems cooperating; compatibility is one fitting another.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Built on written program instructions rather than on ready-made tools.
practiceSentences: The club runs a coding-based course rather than a drag-and-drop one.
Is a coding-based approach harder to start and easier to extend?
A coding-based solution can be changed by anyone who reads it.
They chose a coding-based tool so the school could adapt it.
Coding-based means somebody wrote the instructions rather than clicked them.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Decided by what the measurements show rather than by opinion.
practiceSentences: The timetable change was data-driven and unpopular.
What makes a decision data-driven rather than data-decorated?
A data-driven decision is only as good as the data behind it.
Their data-driven approach found a problem nobody had reported.
Data-driven follows the evidence; evidence-led admits judgement is still involved.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Connected to other computers so information can be shared.
practiceSentences: Every classroom printer is networked to one server.
What becomes possible once a device is networked?
A networked device is reachable, which is its use and its risk.
The networked sensors reported the flood before anyone saw it.
Networked means connected; standalone means it works alone.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Able to be given instructions that change what it does.
practiceSentences: A programmable thermostat learns the week's pattern.
What makes this device programmable rather than merely adjustable?
A programmable machine can do a job nobody designed it for.
The programmable board cost less than the fixed one.
Programmable takes new instructions; automatic only repeats its own.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: A deliberate attempt to damage or break into a computer system.
practiceSentences: The cyberattack shut the booking system for two days.
How would a school notice a cyberattack early?
A cyberattack often begins with one convincing email.
The hospital's cyberattack delayed operations, not just paperwork.
A cyberattack is the event; cybercrime is the offence.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Criminal activity carried out using computers or networks.
practiceSentences: Cybercrime now costs more than many kinds of theft.
What makes cybercrime difficult to prosecute?
Cybercrime crosses borders faster than the law follows.
The unit investigates cybercrime reported by small businesses.
Cybercrime is the category; a cyberattack is one act within it.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Checking that something is correct or meets its requirements.
practiceSentences: Form validation catches the missing digit before the form is sent.
What validation does this data go through?
Validation checks the input; verification checks the result.
Without validation, one wrong date corrupted the whole export.
Validation also means having your feelings acknowledged, which is a different use.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: To do with the waves that carry light, radio and X-rays.
practiceSentences: Radio and visible light are both electromagnetic waves.
Which electromagnetic waves does this device use?
Electromagnetic waves need no material to travel through.
The whole wireless network runs on electromagnetic radiation.
The electromagnetic spectrum runs from radio waves to gamma rays.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Happening at regular intervals, or arranged in repeating patterns.
practiceSentences: The system runs a periodic backup every night.
What periodic checks does this equipment need?
A periodic signal repeats itself at a fixed rate.
The periodic table arranges elements by repeating properties.
Periodic repeats on a schedule; occasional does not.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: The movement of water through a membrane towards the stronger solution.
practiceSentences: Osmosis moves water into the root without any pumping.
In which direction does osmosis carry the water here?
Osmosis needs a membrane that lets water through and not the dissolved substance.
Reverse osmosis is how some plants make drinking water from the sea.
People say they learned something by osmosis, which is a joke about the word.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: The study of living things too small to see without a microscope.
practiceSentences: Microbiology explains why the water had to be boiled.
What can microbiology tell us that a symptom cannot?
Microbiology became possible only once lenses were good enough.
Her work in microbiology traced the outbreak to one well.
Microbiology studies the organisms; medicine treats what they do.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Using letters to stand for numbers in a rule or formula.
practiceSentences: The algebraic expression works for every value of n.
Which algebraic rule describes this pattern?
An algebraic statement says something about all numbers at once.
She wrote the algebraic form and the pattern became obvious.
Algebraic uses letters; arithmetic uses only numbers.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Growing by a multiplying factor each step, so it accelerates.
practiceSentences: Exponential growth looks slow until it suddenly does not.
Is this growth exponential or merely fast?
An exponential curve doubles in a fixed time, again and again.
The number of connected devices grew exponentially for a decade.
Exponential multiplies each step; linear only adds.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Changing by the same amount each step, so it plots as a straight line.
practiceSentences: The cost is linear: each extra user adds the same amount.
Is this relationship linear across the whole range?
A linear graph is a straight line, whatever its slope.
She fitted a linear model and it held for four years.
Linear adds the same each time; exponential multiplies.

words.group: Grammar: leaving words out, and putting words in their place
words.childMeaning: Leaving out words that the reader can supply from context.
practiceSentences: In she can code and he cannot, ellipsis removes the second code.
Where has ellipsis been used in this sentence?
Ellipsis avoids repeating what has just been said.
Speech uses ellipsis constantly without anyone noticing.
Ellipsis also names the three dots that mark an omission.

words.group: Grammar: leaving words out, and putting words in their place
words.childMeaning: Replacing a word or phrase with a shorter one to avoid repeating it.
practiceSentences: In I have a laptop and she has one too, one is a substitution.
Which word is doing the substitution here?
Substitution replaces; ellipsis removes altogether.
Careful substitution keeps a paragraph from repeating a long noun.
Words like one, do and so are the commonest substitutions in English.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ability
words.childMeaning: A complete and often surprising change in the form, appearance or nature of something.
practiceSentences: The transformation of the draft between March and June was total.
What transformation does the character undergo?
A transformation changes the nature of a thing, not only its surface.
Her transformation as a writer began with cutting adjectives.
In mathematics a transformation moves or resizes a shape.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ability
words.childMeaning: The quality of being well founded and able to stand up to testing.
practiceSentences: The validity of the conclusion rests on one unchecked figure.
How would you test the validity of this argument?
Validity is about the reasoning; truth is about the world.
An argument can have validity and still reach a false conclusion.
A ticket has validity too, which is the everyday use of the word.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ability
words.childMeaning: How much something varies from one measurement to the next.
practiceSentences: The variability between the two seasons made the average useless.
What variability would you expect in this data?
High variability hides a pattern that a mean pretends is there.
She reported the variability alongside the average, as she should.
Variability is how much it changes; a variable is what changes.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: An indirect reference to another work, person or event.
practiceSentences: The title is an allusion to an older poem.
Which allusion opens the second stanza?
An allusion rewards the reader who recognises it and does not punish the one who does not.
The speech was full of allusions to the founding story.
An allusion hints at something; a quotation states it.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Placing two things side by side so the contrast shows.
practiceSentences: The juxtaposition of the wedding and the funeral is deliberate.
What does this juxtaposition make you notice?
Juxtaposition argues without saying anything.
The photograph's juxtaposition of new tower and old well says it all.
Juxtaposition places side by side; comparison discusses the difference.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A statement that seems to contradict itself yet holds a truth.
practiceSentences: The more you explain the joke, the less funny it is: that is a paradox.
Which paradox is the poem built around?
A paradox is not a mistake; it is a truth folded awkwardly.
She ended on a paradox and left the audience arguing.
A paradox seems contradictory; a contradiction simply is.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A speech in which a character alone on stage thinks aloud.
practiceSentences: The soliloquy lets the audience hear what nobody else may.
Where does the soliloquy fall in the play?
A soliloquy is spoken alone; an aside is spoken past the others.
His soliloquy runs to forty lines and changes the whole play.
A soliloquy reveals a mind; a dialogue reveals a relationship.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To do with the meaning of words.
practiceSentences: The disagreement was semantic: they meant different things by fair.
What semantic difference separates these two words?
A semantic field groups words that share a subject.
She traced the semantic shift of the word across two centuries.
Semantic is about meaning; syntactic is about arrangement.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The arrangement of words to make a well-formed sentence.
practiceSentences: The syntax is correct even where the meaning is not.
What does the poet's unusual syntax achieve?
Syntax decides what a sentence can mean before any word is chosen.
Inverted syntax slows a reader down, which may be the point.
Syntax is the order; semantics is the meaning.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The voice a poem is written in, which is not the poet.
practiceSentences: The speaker of the poem is a soldier, not the poet herself.
What do we learn about the speaker from the first line?
The speaker is a character the poet invents, sometimes unlike them entirely.
Confusing the speaker with the poet is the commonest mistake in essays.
Speaker also means anybody talking, which is why this use has to be taught.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A short, sharp saying that makes its point wittily.
practiceSentences: The essay closes on an epigram nobody forgets.
Which epigram would you choose for the title page?
An epigram must be short enough to repeat from memory.
She wrote an epigram where a paragraph had been.
An epigram is witty and brief; a proverb is old and anonymous.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A play in which the main character is brought down, often by their own flaw.
practiceSentences: A tragedy turns on a flaw in the hero rather than on bad luck.
What flaw brings this tragedy about?
A tragedy ends badly by design, and the audience sees it coming.
The play is a tragedy because the fall could have been avoided.
Tragedy also means any terrible event, which is the everyday use.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To show that two things change together.
practiceSentences: The two sets of readings correlate closely.
Does reading time correlate with the results here?
Two things can correlate without either causing the other.
She correlated the rainfall with the harvest over ten years.
To correlate is to move together; to cause is another claim entirely.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To add a limit to a statement so it is not too broad.
practiceSentences: Qualify the claim before somebody else does it for you.
How would you qualify this conclusion?
To qualify a statement is to make it defensible, not to weaken it.
She qualified every finding with the size of the sample.
Qualify also means to become eligible, as for a competition.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To prove that a statement is wrong.
practiceSentences: One counterexample was enough to refute the rule.
What evidence would refute this claim?
To refute is to disprove, not merely to deny.
He refuted the argument and conceded the conclusion.
Refute needs evidence; reject needs only an opinion.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To support a claim with evidence.
practiceSentences: Substantiate each assertion or remove it.
What would substantiate this figure?
To substantiate is to show the working, not to repeat the claim.
The article failed to substantiate its most quoted sentence.
Substantiate provides evidence; assert provides none.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To name things one by one in order.
practiceSentences: Enumerate the reasons before you rank them.
Can you enumerate the steps in the argument?
To enumerate is to list with a number attached.
She enumerated four objections and answered three.
Enumerate names each one; summarise gathers them together.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To take an argument or text apart to see how it works.
practiceSentences: Deconstruct the advertisement before you judge it.
How would you deconstruct this opening paragraph?
To deconstruct is to expose the assumptions holding a thing up.
She deconstructed the speech line by line.
To deconstruct is to take apart; to destroy is not the same word.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Using a grid of numbered axes to give a position.
practiceSentences: Cartesian coordinates give every point a pair of numbers.
Which Cartesian quadrant is this point in?
The Cartesian plane has an x axis and a y axis crossing at zero.
She plotted the results on Cartesian axes.
Cartesian is named after Descartes, which is why it keeps its capital.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A fixed relationship in which one quantity scales with another.
practiceSentences: The graph shows proportionality between distance and time.
Is there proportionality across the whole range?
Proportionality means doubling one doubles the other.
The recipe relies on proportionality, so it scales to any number.
Proportionality is a constant ratio; correlation need not be.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Describing an expression in which the highest power is two.
practiceSentences: A quadratic equation has at most two solutions.
Which term makes this equation quadratic?
A quadratic graph is a curve, never a straight line.
She solved the quadratic by completing the square.
Quadratic means squared; linear means to the first power.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Happening or being solved at the same time.
practiceSentences: Simultaneous equations are solved together, not one after the other.
What makes these two equations simultaneous?
Two simultaneous equations share a solution that fits both.
The simultaneous broadcasts reached four countries at once.
Simultaneous means at once; consecutive means one then the next.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A statement in mathematics that has been proved from other truths.
practiceSentences: The theorem holds for every right-angled triangle.
Which theorem would you use here?
A theorem is proved once and then relied on for ever.
She quoted the theorem rather than reproving it.
A theorem is proved; a conjecture is only believed.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Imagined for the sake of argument rather than real.
practiceSentences: Take a hypothetical class of thirty and work it through.
Is that a hypothetical case or one that happened?
A hypothetical example tests an argument without accusing anyone.
She answered the hypothetical question and refused the real one.
Hypothetical is supposed for argument; theoretical rests on a theory.

words.group: Grammar: the two ways to describe a word's behaviour
words.childMeaning: To do with the words of a language rather than its grammar.
practiceSentences: The lexical choice between slim and skinny carries the whole judgement.
What lexical field does this poem draw on?
A lexical change alters which words are used, not how they are arranged.
She studied the lexical differences between the two translations.
Lexical is about vocabulary; syntactic is about structure.

words.group: Grammar: the two ways to describe a word's behaviour
words.childMeaning: To do with how words are arranged in a sentence.
practiceSentences: The syntactic structure changes where the emphasis falls.
What syntactic feature makes this sentence hard to read?
A syntactic error breaks the sentence; a lexical one only misnames.
The poet's syntactic inversions slow the reader deliberately.
Syntactic concerns arrangement; semantic concerns meaning.
